proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \((p,k,m,M,s,V)\in\mathfrak T\) and \(P\in\mathcal M_{p,k}(m,M,s,V)\).  For \(a\in\mathcal I_2\), treatment overlap \(0<\pi<1\), which is part of Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}gaussian\text{-}margin\text{-}class}\), makes the observed conditional arm law
\[
 Q_a=\mathcal L_P(X,Y\mid A=a)
\]
well defined.  On the event \(\{A=a\}\), the consistency equation \(Y=AY_1+(1-A)Y_0\) gives \(Y=Y_a\).  Hence, for all Borel sets \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^p\) and \(D\subseteq\mathbb R\),
\[
 Q_a(C\times D)
 =P(X\in C,Y_a\in D\mid A=a)
 =P(X\in C,Y_a\in D).
\]
The second equality is exactly Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}randomized\text{-}assignment}\), because \(A\perp(X,Y_0,Y_1)\) implies \(A\perp(X,Y_a)\).  Taking \(D=\mathbb R\) yields
\[
 Q_0(C\times\mathbb R)=P(X\in C)=Q_1(C\times\mathbb R).
\]
Thus the two observed arm laws have the same pretreatment-covariate marginal.  This is the membership requirement in the information model \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{Lin}}\); consequently \(P\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{Lin}}\).  Since \(P\) was arbitrary,
\[
 \mathcal M_{p,k}(m,M,s,V)\subseteq\mathcal M_{\mathrm{Lin}}.
\]

It remains to show that the inclusion is proper for every admissible tuple.  Fix the same \(p\) and let \(P^\star\) be the law under which \(A\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\), the coordinates \(X_1,\ldots,X_p\) are mutually independent with
\[
 P^\star(X_j=1)=P^\star(X_j=-1)=\tfrac12,
\]
and \(Y_0,Y_1\) are independent \(N(0,1)\) variables, with \(A\), \(X\), \(Y_0\), and \(Y_1\) mutually independent.  The two observed arm laws under \(P^\star\) are \(\mathcal L_{P^\star}(X,Y_0)\) and \(\mathcal L_{P^\star}(X,Y_1)\), and both have the displayed Rademacher product law as their \(X\)-marginal.  Therefore \(P^\star\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{Lin}}\) by the definition of that information model.

On the other hand, \((X,Y_a)\) is not jointly Gaussian for either \(a\).  Indeed, if it were jointly Gaussian, the coordinate projection \(X_j=e_j^{\mathsf T}(X,Y_a)\) would be Gaussian by the defining property that every linear functional of a jointly Gaussian vector is univariate Gaussian.  But \(X_j\) has variance one and two atoms of mass \(1/2\), whereas a nondegenerate univariate Gaussian law has no atoms.  Hence Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}joint\text{-}gaussian\text{-}arms}\), which is a membership condition in Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}gaussian\text{-}margin\text{-}class}\), fails for \(P^\star\).  Thus
\[
 P^\star\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{Lin}}\setminus\mathcal M_{p,k}(m,M,s,V),
\]
which proves \(\mathcal M_{p,k}(m,M,s,V)\subsetneq\mathcal M_{\mathrm{Lin}}\) for every \((p,k,m,M,s,V)\in\mathfrak T\).

Fix an admissible tuple and \(P\in\mathcal M_{p,k}(m,M,s,V)\), and fix \(S\) with \(|S|\leq 2k\).  The sparse-spectrum assumption gives \(\Sigma_{SS}\succeq mI\), so \(Q_S:=\Sigma_{SS}^{-1}\) exists.  By joint Gaussianity,
\[
 \mathcal L_P(Y_a\mid X_S)
 =\mathcal N\!\left(\mu_a+c_{a,S}^{\mathsf T}Q_S(X_S-\mu_{X,S}),\ r_a(S)\right),
 \qquad a\in\{0,1\}.
\]
The residual-floor assumption makes both conditional variances positive.  Randomized assignment identifies each marginal law \(\mathcal L_P(X_S,Y_a)\) from the arm-\(a\) observed law; it does not identify the conditional coupling of \(Y_0\) and \(Y_1\).

Put \(m_a(x)=\mu_a+c_{a,S}^{\mathsf T}Q_S(x-\mu_{X,S})\).  For any coupling of the two displayed conditional laws, conditional Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
 \mathbb E\{(Y_1-Y_0)^2\mid X_S=x\}
 \geq \{m_1(x)-m_0(x)\}^2+
 \{\sqrt{r_1(S)}-\sqrt{r_0(S)}\}^2.
\]
Indeed, after centering, the cross moment is at most
\(\sqrt{r_0(S)r_1(S)}\).  Equality is attained by taking a standard normal \(Z_*\), independent of \(X_S\), and setting
\[
 Y_a=m_a(X_S)+\sqrt{r_a(S)}Z_*,\qquad a\in\{0,1\}.
\]
This construction preserves both identified retained marginals.  Thus, if \(\Theta_I^S(P)\) denotes the values of \(\tau_2\) generated by all couplings preserving those two marginals, every \(\tau_2\in\Theta_I^S(P)\) satisfies \(\tau_2\geq B(S)\), and the displayed common-residual coupling attains equality.  Hence \(B(S)\) is the sharp lower endpoint; it is not being equated by definition with the causal target.

It remains to integrate the conditional-mean term.  Since
\(\operatorname{Var}(X_S)=\Sigma_{SS}\),
\[
 \mathbb E\{m_1(X_S)-m_0(X_S)\}^2
 = (\mu_1-\mu_0)^2
 +(c_{1,S}-c_{0,S})^{\mathsf T}Q_S(c_{1,S}-c_{0,S}).
\]
Adding the attained residual contribution proves the asserted formula.  Expanding its last square and using
\(r_a(S)=v_a-c_{a,S}^{\mathsf T}Q_Sc_{a,S}\) also gives the identity
\[
 B(S)=(\mu_1-\mu_0)^2+v_0+v_1
 -2c_{0,S}^{\mathsf T}Q_Sc_{1,S}
 -2\sqrt{r_0(S)r_1(S)},
\]
which will be used below.

Write \(r_a=r_a(L)\).  The sparse-spectrum and residual-floor assumptions give \(\Sigma_{LL}\succ0\), \(r_a\geq s>0\), and hence every object in the residual-score definition is well defined.  The block inverse formula, applied first quadratically and then bilinearly, yields
\[
 r_a(L\cup T)=r_a-d_a^{\mathsf T}H^{-1}d_a
 =r_a\{1-\|u_a\|_2^2\},
\]
and
\[
 c_{0,L\cup T}^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_{L\cup T,L\cup T}^{-1}c_{1,L\cup T}
 -c_{0,L}^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_{LL}^{-1}c_{1,L}
 =d_0^{\mathsf T}H^{-1}d_1.
\]
For completeness, the bilinear identity follows by applying the quadratic Schur-complement identity to \(c_0+c_1\) and \(c_0-c_1\) and subtracting.  Substitution into the alternative endpoint formula proved in \(\texttt{prop:gaussian-endpoint}\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \Delta(L,T)
 &=2\sqrt{r_0r_1}-2d_0^{\mathsf T}H^{-1}d_1
   -2\sqrt{r_0(L\cup T)r_1(L\cup T)}\\
 &=2\sqrt{r_0r_1}\left[1-u_0^{\mathsf T}u_1
 -\sqrt{(1-\|u_0\|_2^2)(1-\|u_1\|_2^2)}\right]\\
 &=2\sqrt{r_0r_1}\,g(u_0,u_1).
\end{aligned}
\]
Because each \(z(u_a)\) has unit norm and
\(z(u_0)^{\mathsf T}z(u_1)=1-g(u_0,u_1)\), this equals
\(\sqrt{r_0r_1}\|z(u_0)-z(u_1)\|_2^2\), proving the angular identity.

We next prove every asserted side condition.  For \(x\in\mathbb R^{|T|}\), the Schur-complement variational formula is
\[
 x^{\mathsf T}Hx
 =\min_{y\in\mathbb R^{|L|}}
 (y^{\mathsf T},x^{\mathsf T})
 \Sigma_{L\cup T,L\cup T}(y^{\mathsf T},x^{\mathsf T})^{\mathsf T}.
\]
The sparse-spectrum assumption on \(L\cup T\) bounds the right side below by \(m\|x\|_2^2\); choosing \(y=0\) bounds it above by \(M\|x\|_2^2\).  Hence \(mI\preceq H\preceq MI\).  If \(D=\operatorname{diag}(H)\), then \(D\preceq MI\), so \(D^{-1}\succeq M^{-1}I\), and consequently
\[
 H^{1/2}D^{-1}H^{1/2}\succeq M^{-1}H\succeq (m/M)I.
\]
Finally, conditional variances cannot exceed marginal variances, so
\(r_a(L)\leq v_a\leq V\).  Combining the residual update with the residual-floor assumption at \(L\cup T\) gives
\[
 1-\|u_a\|_2^2
 =\frac{r_a(L\cup T)}{r_a(L)}\geq \frac{s}{V},
\]
or \(\|u_a\|_2^2\leq1-s/V\), as required.

Normalization follows immediately from the gain definition: \(F(\varnothing)=0\).  We first verify monotonicity without imposing a hidden residual-positivity condition outside the budget range.  For arbitrary \(L\subseteq S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\}\), let \(T=S\setminus L\), let \(H\) and \(d_a\) be the corresponding Schur-complement quantities, and put \(q_a=H^{-1/2}d_a\).  The block residual identity gives
\(r_a(S)=r_a(L)-\|q_a\|_2^2\geq0\).  The endpoint algebra used in \(\texttt{lem:angular-identity}\), which remains valid when a residual is zero, gives
\[
 B(S)-B(L)=2\left\{\sqrt{r_0(L)r_1(L)}
 -q_0^{\mathsf T}q_1-\sqrt{r_0(S)r_1(S)}\right\}.
\]
The vectors \((q_a^{\mathsf T},\sqrt{r_a(S)})^{\mathsf T}\) have norms \(\sqrt{r_a(L)}\).  Cauchy--Schwarz therefore makes the expression in braces nonnegative.  Thus \(B\), and hence \(F\), is monotone; normalization then implies \(F(S)\geq0\).

It remains to prove the ratio bound.  Fix an eligible disjoint pair \(L,T\) with \(\Delta(L,T)>0\), and abbreviate \(r_a=r_a(L)\), \(D=\operatorname{diag}(H)\), and
\[
 w_j=\frac{H^{1/2}e_j}{\sqrt{H_{jj}}},\qquad j\in T.
\]
Each \(w_j\) is a unit vector and, by \(\texttt{lem:angular-identity}\),
\[
 \sum_{j\in T}w_jw_j^{\mathsf T}
 =H^{1/2}D^{-1}H^{1/2}\succeq(m/M)I.
\]
The normalized singleton residual score is exactly
\[
 \frac{d_{a,j}}{\sqrt{H_{jj}}\sqrt{r_a}}=w_j^{\mathsf T}u_a;
\]
this equality is the step that retains coordinate meaning after joint whitening.

We use the following elementary hemisphere comparison.  If
\(\|u\|_2,\|v\|_2\leq\sqrt{1-q}\) with \(0<q\leq1\), then
\[
 \frac12\|u-v\|_2^2\leq g(u,v)
 \leq\frac{1}{2q}\|u-v\|_2^2.
\]
The lower inequality is obtained by discarding the final nonnegative square in
\(2g(u,v)=\|u-v\|_2^2+\{\sqrt{1-\|u\|_2^2}-\sqrt{1-\|v\|_2^2}\}^2\).
For the upper inequality, the gradient of \(x\mapsto\sqrt{1-\|x\|_2^2}\) on the convex ball of radius \(\sqrt{1-q}\) has norm at most \(\sqrt{(1-q)/q}\).  Integration along the line segment from \(u\) to \(v\) bounds the last square by \((1-q)\|u-v\|_2^2/q\).  The case \(q=1\) is immediate.

Apply this comparison with \(q=s/V\), which is permitted by the radius conclusion of \(\texttt{lem:angular-identity}\), and put \(\delta=u_0-u_1\).  The singleton angular identities, the lower hemisphere inequality, and the frame bound give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \sum_{j\in T}\Delta(L,\{j\})
 &=2\sqrt{r_0r_1}\sum_{j\in T}
   g(w_j^{\mathsf T}u_0,w_j^{\mathsf T}u_1)\\
 &\geq\sqrt{r_0r_1}\sum_{j\in T}(w_j^{\mathsf T}\delta)^2\\
 &\geq\sqrt{r_0r_1}(m/M)\|\delta\|_2^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
The joint angular identity and the upper hemisphere inequality give
\[
 \Delta(L,T)\leq\sqrt{r_0r_1}(V/s)\|\delta\|_2^2.
\]
Positivity of \(\Delta(L,T)\) forces \(\delta\neq0\), so division is legitimate and yields
\[
 \frac{\sum_{j\in T}\Delta(L,\{j\})}{\Delta(L,T)}
 \geq\frac{m}{M}\frac{s}{V}=\Gamma=\frac1{KR}.
\]
Taking the infimum and applying the cap at one in the definition of \(\gamma_k\) proves the claim, since \(0<\Gamma\leq1\).  Neither the comparison nor its constants depend on \(p\) or \(k\).

Fix \(k\geq2\), \(K\geq1\), \(R>1\), and \(\eta>0\).  In the family of \(\texttt{def:extremal-family}\), write \(e=\mathbf1_k/\sqrt{k}\) and
\(\Sigma_{\mathrm{act}}=KI_k-(K-1)ee^{\mathsf T}\).  This matrix has eigenvalue \(1\) along \(e\) and eigenvalue \(K\) on \(e^\perp\); after adjoining the \(k\) independent dummy coordinates, the full covariance has spectrum in \([1,K]\).  Every principal submatrix therefore has all eigenvalues in \([1,K]\), by its Rayleigh quotients, proving the required sparse-spectrum restriction with \(m=1\) and \(M=K\).

Let \(Z_*=e^{\mathsf T}X_{1:k}\).  Since \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{act}}e=e\), \(\operatorname{Var}(Z_*)=1\).  For every coordinate set \(S\), independence of the arm noise gives
\[
 r_0(S)=1+(R-1)\operatorname{Var}(Z_*\mid X_S),\qquad
 r_1(S)=1+(R-h-1)\operatorname{Var}(Z_*\mid X_S).
\]
Thus both residuals are at least one for every \(S\), in particular for every \(|S|\leq2k\).  Also \(v_0=R\) and \(v_1=R-h\in(1,R)\), so the variance ceiling holds.  Randomized assignment and joint Gaussianity hold by construction.  Consequently \(P_h\in\mathcal M_{2k,k}(1,K,1,R)\) for every \(h\in(0,R-1)\).

The arm variances are unequal.  If \(S\) is a proper subset of the active coordinates, positive definiteness of \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{act}}\) and the nonzero coefficient of each omitted active coordinate imply
\(\operatorname{Var}(Z_*\mid X_S)>0\).  Hence
\(r_0(S)-r_1(S)=h\operatorname{Var}(Z_*\mid X_S)>0\), proving unequal conditional scales on every proper active subset.

Take \(L=\varnothing\) and \(T=\{1,\ldots,k\}\).  Define
\[
 a=\sqrt{1-1/R},\qquad b_h=\sqrt{1-1/(R-h)},\qquad
 t=\frac{1}{1+(k-1)K}.
\]
The joint scores are \(u_0=ae\) and \(u_1=b_he\).  Moreover
\(\Sigma_{jj}=\{1+(k-1)K\}/k\) and \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{act}}^{1/2}e=e\), so the normalized coordinate frame satisfies \(w_j^{\mathsf T}e=\sqrt t\).  Therefore the eligible positive-denominator ratio for this pair is exactly
\[
 Q_h=\frac{k\,g_1(\sqrt t\,a,\sqrt t\,b_h)}{g_1(a,b_h)},
 \qquad
 g_1(x,y)=\frac12\left[(x-y)^2+
 \{\sqrt{1-x^2}-\sqrt{1-y^2}\}^2\right].
\]
Here \(b_h\neq a\) for \(h>0\), so its denominator is positive.  For \(|x|<1\), direct differentiation of the upper semicircle parametrization gives
\[
 \lim_{y\to x}\frac{g_1(x,y)}{(x-y)^2}=\frac{1}{2(1-x^2)}.
\]
Since \(b_h\to a\) as \(h\downarrow0\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \lim_{h\downarrow0}Q_h
 &=k\,\frac{t(1-a^2)}{1-ta^2}\\
 &=\frac{k}{1+(k-1)KR}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Continuity therefore supplies a sufficiently small \(h\in(0,R-1)\) for which
\(Q_h\leq k/[1+(k-1)KR]+\eta\).  Since \(\gamma_k\) is the infimum over eligible pairs, \(\gamma_k(F;P_h)\leq Q_h\), proving the displayed upper bound.

The construction also proves both necessity and dimension-free optimality.  Holding \(R>1\) fixed and allowing \(K\) to grow makes the attainable ratio of order \(K^{-1}\); holding \(K\) fixed and allowing \(R\) to grow makes it of order \(R^{-1}\).  Thus neither factor can be removed from a uniform certificate.  More exactly, suppose \(c(K,R)\) is any lower certificate valid for every dimension and every admissible budget with these margins.  Applying it to the displayed family for each \(k\), then sending \(h\downarrow0\), gives
\[
 c(K,R)\leq\frac{k}{1+(k-1)KR}.
\]
Sending \(k\to\infty\) gives \(c(K,R)\leq1/(KR)\).  The theorem \(\texttt{thm:dimension-free-frontier}\) proves the reverse uniform inequality, so \(1/(KR)\) is the largest certificate depending only on \((K,R)\) uniformly over dimensions and budgets.

Let \(S^*\in\arg\max_{|S|\leq k}F(S)\), which exists because the ground set is finite.  Write \(S_i\) for the population greedy set after \(i\) steps and \(G_i=\mathrm{OPT}-F(S_i)\).  If \(G_i\leq0\), monotonicity makes the desired bound immediate.  Otherwise set \(T_i=S^*\setminus S_i\).  Monotonicity and the submodularity-ratio bound from \(\texttt{thm:dimension-free-frontier}\) give
\[
 \sum_{j\in T_i}\{F(S_i\cup\{j\})-F(S_i)\}
 \geq\Gamma\{F(S_i\cup S^*)-F(S_i)\}
 \geq\Gamma G_i.
\]
There are at most \(k\) terms.  The greedy marginal is therefore at least \(\Gamma G_i/k\), so
\(G_{i+1}\leq(1-\Gamma/k)G_i\).  Since \(F(\varnothing)=0\), iteration yields
\[
 F(S_g)\geq\left\{1-\left(1-\frac\Gamma k\right)^k\right\}\mathrm{OPT}.
\]
The elementary inequality \(1-x\leq e^{-x}\), applied at \(x=\Gamma/k\), gives the second population bound.

Now work on the stated event of uniform endpoint error and let \(\widehat S_i\) be the empirical greedy path.  For every candidate \(j\notin\widehat S_i\), both evaluated sets have size at most \(k\), and hence
\[
 \left|\{\widehat F(\widehat S_i\cup\{j\})-\widehat F(\widehat S_i)\}
 -\{F(\widehat S_i\cup\{j\})-F(\widehat S_i)\}\right|\leq2\epsilon.
\]
Maximizing the estimated marginal can consequently lose at most \(4\epsilon\) relative to the largest true marginal.  Repeating the preceding ratio argument at \(\widehat S_i\) gives
\[
 \mathrm{OPT}-F(\widehat S_{i+1})
 \leq\left(1-\frac\Gamma k\right)
 \{\mathrm{OPT}-F(\widehat S_i)\}+4\epsilon.
\]
After \(k\) iterations,
\[
 F(\widehat S)\geq
 \left\{1-\left(1-\frac\Gamma k\right)^k\right\}\mathrm{OPT}
 -4\epsilon\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}(1-\Gamma/k)^i
 \geq
 \left\{1-\left(1-\frac\Gamma k\right)^k\right\}\mathrm{OPT}-4k\epsilon.
\]
This proves both claims using the generic greedy recurrence; the model-specific input is exactly the proved value of \(\Gamma\).

Fix the displayed constants and \(p,k\).  We first prove compactness of the parameter image.  The mean-envelope assumption bounds \(\mu_X,\mu_0,\mu_1\).  The singleton sparse-spectrum bounds give \(m\leq\Sigma_{jj}\leq M\), while positive semidefiniteness gives \(|\Sigma_{j\ell}|\leq\sqrt{\Sigma_{jj}\Sigma_{\ell\ell}}\leq M\).  The residual floor at the empty set and the variance ceiling give \(s\leq v_a\leq V\).  Finally, covariance Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\(|c_{a,j}|^2\leq\Sigma_{jj}v_a\leq MV\), and treatment overlap puts \(\pi\) in a compact subinterval of \((0,1)\).  Thus \(\Theta\) is bounded.

It is also closed.  Every defining spectral, residual, variance, mean, and overlap inequality is continuous in the finite-dimensional moments because all required covariance inverses have eigenvalues at least \(m\).  A convergent parameter sequence therefore preserves all inequalities.  Its limiting arm covariance blocks are positive semidefinite; one can realize the limiting jointly Gaussian arm marginals by regressing each \(Y_a\) on \(X\) and adding a possibly degenerate Gaussian residual, and then draw \(A\) independently with the limiting overlap probability.  This realizes the limiting parameter within the admissible class.  Hence \(\Theta\) is closed and bounded in finite-dimensional Euclidean space and is compact.

The influence variance \(\nu_S^2(\vartheta)\) is continuous: the coefficients in the displayed influence function are continuous because \(\Sigma_{SS}\succeq mI\), \(r_a(S)\geq s\), and \(\pi\in[\pi_0,1-\pi_0]\), while Gaussian moments are polynomial functions of means and covariance entries.  Since \(\mathcal A\) is finite,
\(\vartheta\mapsto\min_{S\in\mathcal A}\nu_S(\vartheta)\) is continuous.  The Wald-separated image is its closed upper-level set inside compact \(\Theta\), hence is compact.

We next exhibit the inverse of the raw-moment map.  From \(Q(\vartheta)\), recover
\[
 \pi=\mathbb E[A],\quad
 \mu_X=\mathbb E[X],\quad
 \Sigma=\mathbb E[XX^{\mathsf T}]-\mu_X\mu_X^{\mathsf T}.
\]
Writing \(\pi_1=\pi\) and \(\pi_0'=1-\pi\), recover, for \(a\in\{0,1\}\),
\[
 \mu_a=\frac{\mathbb E[I_aY]}{\pi_a},\qquad
 c_a=\frac{\mathbb E[I_aXY]}{\pi_a}-\mu_X\mu_a,
 \qquad
 v_a=\frac{\mathbb E[I_aY^2]}{\pi_a}-\mu_a^2.
\]
These formulas prove injectivity.  Both \(Q\) and this inverse are continuous because the overlap denominators are bounded below by \(\pi_0\).

For each \(S\in\mathcal A\), the formula defining \(b_S\) is continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood of \(\Theta\): compactness and the uniform margins permit a common neighborhood on which \(\pi\), the eigenvalues of \(\Sigma_{SS}\), and both residual variances remain bounded away from zero.  The inverse map and square root are continuously differentiable there.

Finally, Gaussian fourth-moment formulas make \(\Omega(\vartheta)\) continuous.  Each coordinate of \(Z\) has strictly positive variance at every \(\vartheta\in\Theta\).  For \(A\) this follows from overlap; for \(X_j\) and \(X_jX_\ell\) it follows from the nondegenerate Gaussian law of \(X\); and for the arm-weighted coordinates it follows from positive arm probability together with \(v_a\geq s\) and the positive conditional variance \(r_a(\{j\})\geq s\), which make the relevant Gaussian polynomial nonconstant.  Continuity and compactness therefore imply
\[
 \inf_{\vartheta\in\Theta}\min_{1\leq j\leq d_p}\Omega_{jj}(\vartheta)>0.
\]
All conclusions follow.

Fix \(S\in\mathcal A\) and abbreviate
\(\Delta_\mu=\mu_1-\mu_0\), \(\beta_a=\Sigma_{SS}^{-1}c_{a,S}\),
\(t=\sqrt{r_1(S)/r_0(S)}\), and
\(w=\sqrt t\,\beta_0-\beta_1/\sqrt t\).  The endpoint formula in
\(\texttt{prop:gaussian-endpoint}\) is a sum of three nonnegative quantities, and \(\Sigma_{SS}\succ0\).  Consequently
\[
 b_S(\vartheta)=0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \Delta_\mu=0,\quad \beta_0=\beta_1,\quad r_0(S)=r_1(S).
\]
Under these three equalities, \(t=1\) and \(w=0\), so every term in the defined influence function vanishes and \(\nu_S^2(\vartheta)=0\).

Conversely, suppose \(\nu_S^2(\vartheta)=0\).  The influence function is centered, hence it equals zero almost surely.  Conditional on either treatment arm, \((x_S,e_a)\) has a strictly positive Gaussian density on \(\mathbb R^{|S|+1}\), because the sparse-spectrum and residual-floor assumptions give \(\Sigma_{SS}\succ0\) and \(r_a(S)>0\).  The arm-specific expression for the influence function is a polynomial of degree at most two in \((x_S,e_a)\).  A polynomial vanishing almost surely under a positive density vanishes identically.

In arm zero, the coefficient of \(e_0^2\) is \((1-t)/(1-\pi)\); overlap therefore forces \(t=1\).  With \(t=1\), the coefficient vector of \(x_Se_0\) is \(2w/(1-\pi)\), so \(w=0\), and then the coefficient of \(e_0\) is \(-2\Delta_\mu/(1-\pi)\), so \(\Delta_\mu=0\).  The relations \(t=1\) and \(w=0\) are respectively \(r_0(S)=r_1(S)\) and \(\beta_0=\beta_1\).  This proves the equivalence.  By the definition of \(\Theta_+(\nu_*)\), any parameter with \(b_S=0\) for a selectable \(S\) has minimum selectable influence standard deviation zero and is excluded for every \(\nu_*>0\).

Fix \(\nu_*>0\) and work uniformly over \(\vartheta\in\Theta_+(\nu_*)\) and the finite family \(S\in\mathcal A\).  Differentiating the alternative endpoint expression from \(\texttt{prop:gaussian-endpoint}\), with
\(t_S=\sqrt{r_1(S)/r_0(S)}\) and
\(w_S=\sqrt{t_S}\beta_0(S)-\beta_1(S)/\sqrt{t_S}\), gives
\[
\begin{gathered}
 \partial_{\mu_1}b_S=2(\mu_1-\mu_0),\qquad
 \partial_{\mu_0}b_S=-2(\mu_1-\mu_0),\\
 \partial_{v_0}b_S=1-t_S,\qquad
 \partial_{v_1}b_S=1-t_S^{-1},\\
 \partial_{c_0}b_S=2\sqrt{t_S}\,w_S,\qquad
 \partial_{c_1}b_S=-2w_S/\sqrt{t_S},\qquad
 \partial_{\Sigma}b_S=-w_Sw_S^{\mathsf T}.
\end{gathered}
\]
The final identity follows by expanding
\(-w_Sw_S^{\mathsf T}\) and collecting the differentials of the two residual variances and the cross term.  The influence functions of the arm means, variances, and cross-covariances are obtained from their ratio-of-raw-moment formulas, while the pooled covariance influence function is
\(x_Sx_S^{\mathsf T}-\Sigma_{SS}\).  Substitution into the displayed differential gives exactly the function \(\psi_S\) in \(\texttt{def:endpoint-influence}\).

By \(\texttt{prop:parameter-image-regularity}\), the raw-moment-to-endpoint map has uniformly bounded second derivatives on a common neighborhood of \(\Theta\).  The evaluation estimator is a smooth function of the sample mean of the finite vector \(Z\).  Uniformly bounded Gaussian moments and treatment overlap imply, by coordinatewise second-moment bounds, that the sample raw moments differ from their expectations by \(O_{P_\vartheta}(n_2^{-1/2})\), uniformly in \(\vartheta\).  Taylor's formula therefore yields
\[
 \sqrt{n_2}\{\widehat B(S)-b_S(\vartheta)\}
 =n_2^{-1/2}\sum_{i\in D_2}\psi_S(O_i;\vartheta)+o_{P_\vartheta}(1)
\]
uniformly over \(\vartheta\) and \(S\in\mathcal A\).

We justify the uniform normal approximation explicitly.  For any sequence
\((\vartheta_n,S_n)\) in the displayed domain, let
\(W_{n,i}=\psi_{S_n}(O_i;\vartheta_n)/\nu_{S_n}(\vartheta_n)\).  These variables are row-wise independent, centered, and standardized.  Gaussian polynomial moments, compactness, and the lower bound \(\nu_{S_n}\geq\nu_*\) give
\(\sup_n\mathbb E|W_{n,1}|^3<\infty\).  Hence, for each \(\delta>0\),
\[
 \mathbb E\!\left[W_{n,1}^2\mathbf1\{|W_{n,1}|>\delta\sqrt{n_2}\}\right]
 \leq\frac{\mathbb E|W_{n,1}|^3}{\delta\sqrt{n_2}}\longrightarrow0.
\]
The cited Lindeberg--Feller theorem \(\texttt{lem:lindeberg-feller-standardized}\) gives convergence of every such standardized row sum to \(\mathcal N(0,1)\).  The sequential characterization of a uniform limit then makes this convergence uniform over \(\Theta_+(\nu_*)\) and the finite candidate family.

The plug-in influence coefficients converge uniformly by continuity and raw-moment consistency.  Expanding the empirical second moment of the plug-in influence function, and applying Chebyshev's inequality using uniformly bounded fourth moments, gives
\(\widehat\nu_S^2/\nu_S^2\to1\) in probability uniformly.  Combining this ratio consistency with the preceding normal approximation by a two-sided probability sandwich proves uniform studentization and hence uniform fixed-\(S\) Wald coverage \(1-\alpha+o(1)\).

By the independent-split assumption, conditional on \(D_1\), the random \(\widehat S\) is a fixed member of \(\mathcal A\) and \(D_2\) retains law \(P_\vartheta^{n_2}\).  Thus the absolute conditional coverage error is bounded by the maximum of the fixed-\(S\) errors.  Taking the essential supremum over \(D_1\) and then the supremum over \(\vartheta\) proves the asserted conditional coverage statement.

Fix a coordinate \(j\) of \(Z\), and write
\(\omega_j^2(\vartheta)=\Omega_{jj}(\vartheta)\).  The regularity proposition gives a uniform positive lower bound for \(\omega_j^2\); compact Gaussian moment bounds give a uniform bound on the third and fourth centered moments of \(Z_j\).  Along any parameter sequence \(\vartheta_n\in\Theta\), the standardized row variables satisfy the Lindeberg condition by the same third-moment truncation bound used in \(\texttt{thm:split-wald}\).  The cited Lindeberg--Feller theorem \(\texttt{lem:lindeberg-feller-standardized}\) therefore gives a standard-normal limit, uniformly over \(\Theta\) by the sequential characterization.  Chebyshev's inequality and the uniform fourth-moment bound give uniform consistency of the coordinate sample variance.  A probability sandwich then yields
\[
 \inf_{\vartheta\in\Theta}
 P_\vartheta\!\left(
 |\widehat q_j-Q_j(\vartheta)|
 \leq z_{1-\alpha/(2d_p)}\widehat\omega_j/\sqrt{n_2}
 \right)\geq1-\alpha/d_p-o(1).
\]
There are finitely many coordinates, so the union bound implies
\[
 \inf_{\vartheta\in\Theta}P_\vartheta\{\vartheta\in C\}
 \geq1-\alpha-o(1).
\]

On the event \(\vartheta\in C\), the set \(C\) is nonempty and, simultaneously for every \(S\in\mathcal A\),
\[
 \inf_{\xi\in C}b_S(\xi)\leq b_S(\vartheta)
 \leq\sup_{\xi\in C}b_S(\xi).
\]
If \(C\) is empty, the definition returns the full known range and therefore cannot reduce coverage.  Compactness of \(\Theta\), closedness of \(C\), and continuity of \(b_S\) ensure that all displayed extrema are well defined; the inequalities themselves require only infima and suprema.

Under the independent-split assumption, conditioning on \(D_1\) fixes \(\widehat S\in\mathcal A\) without changing the evaluation-sample law.  The simultaneous event \(\vartheta\in C\) then implies
\(b_{\widehat S}(\vartheta)\in J_{\widehat S}\).  Taking the essential infimum over \(D_1\), the infimum over \(\vartheta\), and the lower limit in \(n_2\) proves coverage at least \(1-\alpha\).  No division by \(\nu_S\) occurs.  In particular, by \(\texttt{prop:endpoint-degeneracy}\), the argument includes every equality parameter where \(b_{\widehat S}=0\) and \(\nu_{\widehat S}=0\), exactly the boundary at which ordinary Wald studentization is unavailable.

added_lemmas.statement: For a row-wise independent triangular array of centered random variables whose row variances sum to one, the Lindeberg condition implies convergence in distribution of the row sums to the standard normal law.

attestation.note: Specialized from the theorem at the cited location; the stable DOI is supplied because a lawful verbatim transcription was not available in the solve context.

proposed.statement:
Fix \(\nu_*>0\) with \(\Theta_+(\nu_*)\ne\varnothing\). For any \(D_1\)-measurable \(\widehat S\in\mathcal A\),
\[
\sqrt{n_2}\{\widehat B(\widehat S)-b_{\widehat S}(\vartheta)\}=n_2^{-1/2}\sum_{i\in D_2}\psi_{\widehat S}(O_i;\vartheta)+o_{P_{\vartheta}}(1)
\]
uniformly over \(\vartheta\in\Theta_+(\nu_*)\), and
\[
\sup_{\vartheta\in\Theta_+(\nu_*)}\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{D_1}\left|P_{\vartheta}\{b_{\widehat S}(\vartheta)\in I_{\widehat S}\mid D_1\}-(1-\alpha)\right|\to0.
\]
proposed.justification: The theorem gives exact conditional post-selection coverage uniformly on the explicitly separated moment subclass where every candidate endpoint has nonzero first-order variance.
proposed.gap: Ji--Lei--Spector already provide generic selection-valid inference, and Lin et al. provide a fixed-target quadratic-COT central limit theorem; this Gaussian specialization supplies the endpoint influence map and its exact degeneracy criterion, not a new generic selection principle.
proposed.consumer: Analysts can report uncertainty for the held-out endpoint selected by any first-sample budget rule on \(\Theta_+(\nu_*)\).

proposed_core_edits.reason: Declare the cited Lindeberg--Feller theorem used by the uniform triangular-array normal approximation.

proposed.statement:
For every \(D_1\)-measurable \(\widehat S\in\mathcal A\), the moment-projection interval obeys
\[
\liminf_{n_2\to\infty}\inf_{\vartheta\in\Theta}\operatorname*{ess\,inf}_{D_1}P_{\vartheta}\{b_{\widehat S}(\vartheta)\in J_{\widehat S}\mid D_1\}\ge1-\alpha.
\]
This whole-image claim includes every equality parameter \(\vartheta\in\Theta\) satisfying \(b_{\widehat S}(\vartheta)=0\), for which \(\nu_{\widehat S}^2(\vartheta)=0\) and ordinary Wald inference is unavailable.
proposed.justification: Projection restores honest coverage exactly on the equality boundary where first-order studentization degenerates.
proposed.gap: Imbens--Manski and Stoye address collapsing estimated bounds under regular Gaussian endpoint limits; the proposed interval instead projects primitive Gaussian moments and remains valid when the selected endpoint has zero first derivative.
proposed.consumer: Empirical users obtain a conservative fallback that covers the selected causal lower endpoint over the entire compact moment image \(\Theta\).

proposed_core_edits.reason: Declare the cited Lindeberg--Feller theorem used for the coordinatewise raw-moment confidence region.

open_obligations.what_is_open: Whether every admissible Gaussian objective at one fixed \(k\geq2\) satisfies \(\gamma_k(F)\geq k/[1+(k-1)KR]\), or whether a feasible residual-score frame violates that inequality.
open_obligations.obstruction: The universal proof separately lower-bounds the coordinate chordal losses and upper-bounds the joint chordal loss.  Those two inequalities are jointly sharp only in a growing-budget limit; the frozen assumptions do not force their equality conditions to align at a fixed finite budget.
open_obligations.attempted: The exact singleton-to-joint ratio was reduced to the normalized Schur-complement frame and hemisphere scores.  The radial unequal-scale family attains the proposed rational expression in a vanishing-contrast limit, but optimizing over all feasible nonradial frames and score pairs was not closed without replacing the exact angular losses by the global Lipschitz envelope, which returns only \(1/(KR)\).
open_obligations.partial_result:
The proved universal inequality gives
\[
 \rho_k(K,R)\geq\frac1{KR},
\]
while the legal unequal-scale construction gives, for every fixed \(k\geq2\),
\[
 \rho_k(K,R)\leq\frac{k}{1+(k-1)KR}.
\]
The two bounds coincide as \(k\to\infty\), establishing the exact dimension-free frontier.  Equality at fixed finite \(k\) remains unresolved.
